item.title: Hospitals Brace for Medicaid Work Rules and Deep Funding Cuts
item.description:
Hospitals across the country are mobilizing an expansive outreach effort in an attempt to ensure that roughly 19 million patients do not lose their insurance coverage under new Medicaid work rules that begin in January.

Saying the requirements are generating widespread anxiety and confusion, health care executives are using a variety of methods to help guide the Americans who will be affected. They are deploying staff and volunteers to contact patients with text messages, phone calls and offers of help.

The rules dictate that able-bodied adults without young children either work, volunteer or attend school or job training for at least 80 hours a month. Republicans included the rules last year as part of President Trump’s package of tax cuts and reductions in safety net spending, including nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts.

Hospitals and other health centers are detailing what evidence people in many cases must provide — pay stubs or other proof of work or school attendance — to maintain coverage.

“There’s going to be people who fall through the cracks,” said Nicole Harper, chief financial officer at Eskenazi Health, a safety-net hospital in Indianapolis. “We’re bracing for impact.”

Because hospitals are heavily reliant on Medicaid funding, keeping a stable patient population is critical for them to maintain government reimbursements.

And now that Democrats will assume control of Congress on Jan. 3, some health systems are also preparing lobbying efforts to restore Medicaid cutbacks.

But even with their sizable new majorities, Democrats do not have the votes to override a presidential veto. Unless they strike a deal with Republicans, a rollback of the Medicaid rules and funding cutbacks is uncertain.

Many G.O.P. congressional members have long supported work requirements for Medicaid recipients, contending the system was riddled with fraud and that health insurance should be earned. The government estimates the mandates will save $317 billion in taxpayer spending over 10 years.

By 2034, more than five million low-income people in 44 states and the District of Columbia will lose Medicaid coverage because of the work rules, according to the Congressional Budget Office. Many will fall off by missing filing deadlines and failing to navigate red tape, even if they meet the rules’ criteria, officials and experts said.

Last month, a federal judge in Boston blocked a requirement that would have made it harder for people too sick to work to seek an exemption. Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said on CNBC recently that the ruling would be appealed.

But state and health officials must still review hundreds of serious illnesses and disabilities to decide which patients might qualify.

Complicating matters, the lists of ailments differ from state to state. Nebraska, for instance, has an exemption for rheumatoid arthritis, while Montana does not.

For health systems, the price of patients losing Medicaid coverage is high. Emergency rooms could swell with uninsured patients and hospitals would take a significant financial hit from the loss of reimbursements. More than a third of the nearly $1 trillion in annual Medicaid spending goes to hospitals, paid for withfederal and state taxpayer money.

Safety-net hospitals with large numbers of Medicaid patients warn the financial losses will result in increases in charitable care and uncollected bills, which will shift higher costs to employers and patients with commercial insurance.

Small rural hospitals, which already are operating on thin margins, could be forced to shed jobs and services like maternity wards.

Roseland Community Hospital, a safety-net institution in Chicago, said looming Medicaid cuts were among factors that prompted its bankruptcy filing this month.

Among the people most affected are part-time retail employees, seasonal farm laborers and gig workers like Uber drivers. Many will need to hunt down pay stubs, meet recurring deadlines and fill out complicated eligibility forms.

In Indianapolis, the Eskenazi hospital is dispatchingteams in the city’s low-income neighborhoods to educate patients, Ms. Harper said.

The requirements apply to states that expanded their Medicaid populations under the Affordable Care Act, which allowed childless adults with incomes up to 138 percent of the poverty line to get coverage.

Nebraska and Montana imposed work rules earlier this year, providing a glimpse of what to expect in other states.

After Nebraska imposed mandates in May, wait times on its Medicaid call center rose to as much as two hours from under 30 minutes, according to executives and advocates.

Nebraska’s monthly Medicaid approvals fell 25 percent, or nearly 1,400 people, in May, June and July, according to an analysis of publicly available data by The Hilltop Institute, a nonpartisan research group at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County.

The state’s health centers also reported an increase in uninsured patients.

State officials said in an email that Nebraska denied Medicaid coverage to 1,773 people through September based on work rules alone. They said additional denials across other categories were caused by “seasonal fluctuations” and that it would be premature to attribute them to policy changes.

“Nebraska prepared carefully before launching work requirements on May 1, including training eligibility staff; communicating with community partners; and sending more than 75,000 notices, 38,000 text messages and 10,000 emails,” said Collin Spilinek, a spokesman for the state’s Department of Health and Human Services.

In Montana, which started applying the rules in October, experts said confusion is widespread. They cited state notification letters with conflicting deadlines and a website they found difficult to navigate.

To qualify for a medical exemption in Montana, people must select an ailment from a list of hundreds of permissible diagnoses.

Montana’s list includes kuru, a neurodegenerative disease originating in the South Pacific that is virtually extinct, according to a scientific paper, which notes: “The end of cannibalism has put an end to this disease.”

Nebraska’s diagnoses list also includes kuru but is more encompassing.

“Nebraska has a very exhaustive list that we feel is overly inclusive,” said Rebecca de Camara, Montana’s Medicaid director, said at a legislative hearing in June. “We are trying to have a fairly narrow list that we believe really constitutes medical frailty.”

Montana Medicaid officials did not respond to requests for comment.

Officials and community leaders from Pennsylvania to California say they are moving quickly to prepare for a deadline crush at year’s end.

“It’s going to be a big train wreck,” said Sara Singer, a Stanford University health policy professor and member of a Northern California coalition using artificial intelligence to identify patients at risk of losing coverage.

Community health executives are worried that state Medicaid managers are not fully prepared as the clock ticks down. States have scrambled to issue new contracts to vendors and build systems to scoop up data from multiple government sources, said Matthew Salo, a consultant and past president of the National Association of Medicaid Administrators.

“There really wasn’t enough time to roll out something that was this complex,” he said.

Indiana, which adopted tougher deadlines and procedures than Congress, including quarterly compliance checks, is hiring 400 workers as part of $43 million a year in new spending to manage the new rules, said its Medicaid director, Audrey Frenzel.

Hospital executives in Nebraska said they expected problems to intensify. Since May, 90 percent of the state’s Medicaid denials were attributed to incomplete or improperly filed paperwork, said Jeremy Nordquist, chief executive of the Nebraska Hospital Association.

“That shows that we all have a lot of work left to make sure folks understand what they have to do to keep their coverage,” he said.

Nebraska’s Medicaid agency said that 83 percent of coverage denials for new applications were for people who did not respond to requests for information.

Drew Gonshorowski, who stepped down as the state’s Medicaid director in August and supports work rules, said eligibility checks occur on the anniversary of the original enrollment, which would soften the impact by spreading the burden over the year.

“Regardless of the views on the specific policy, there is opportunity to do what Medicaid programs do really well: extend a hand to the most vulnerable,” he said.

In 2018, Arkansas was the first state to try work mandates under Medicaid, resulting in the loss of insurance for 18,000 people before a federal judge suspended the program.

A survey published in The New England Journal of Medicine found that the program was “plagued by confusion,” noting that 92 percent of those who lost insurance had actually met the work requirement or should have been exempt.

Many of the 19 million adults who are subject to the work requirements can be automatically requalified using state income-tax data systems and other digital sources, according to state Medicaid directors. Others can expect a twice-yearly check-in.

“This is a little like having a D.M.V. appointment to try to prove you’re meeting your work requirements every month,” said Shelly Schlenker, executive vice president for CommonSpirit Health, a system with hospitals in 24 states. “If you’re already struggling to make ends meet, it’s one more burden in your life.”

Sanford Health, the nation’s largest rural health system based in Sioux Falls, S.D., said it was identifying opportunities in its 60 hospitals and 145 nursing homes for recipients to volunteer as valets or patient aides to maintain benefits.

In Michigan, the Henry Ford Health provider network assigned a four-person team a list of 1,400 Medicaid recipients to contact by phone last month, said Raquel Fenderson, who helps patients navigate the system.

People are asking: “How do I qualify, do I qualify?’’’ she said. “I tell them the process is still very new and we don’t have all the information.”

item.title: $150 for Pie? A Humble Thanksgiving Staple Gets Pricey.
item.description:
Bakers in the 18th century who poured stewed pumpkin sweetened with molasses into a rough, thick crust could hardly have imagined their fellow citizens paying more than $100 for a Thanksgiving pie.

But here we are.

What may be this season’s most expensive pie is built on a crust made with Cinnamon Toast Crunch cereal. Its apple custard filling is swirled with apple cider caramel. On top, a sprinkle of gold leaf crowns sour cream rosettes. New York magazine declared it the best pie to order this Thanksgiving. A 12-inch version will set you back just $150.

“I was like, you know what? Why don’t we just up the ante and start making pies more complicated, because I knew how to make them more complicated,” said Michelle Kogan, the New York chef who created the pricey pie.

In San Francisco’s Chinatown, the noted pastry chef Melissa Chou is selling a 10-inch Thanksgiving pie made with toasted wildflower honey custard on a delicate Italian pastry crust, topped with a beeswax-infused sabayon, for $120.

In the Hamptons, New Yorkers can order Lena Kristy’s brown butter apple streusel pie or cranberry pecan pie for $80. Both use jam from her shop, Jamagansett, where her $100 salty blueberry pie went viral over the summer. The ensuing snark prompted her to drop the price to $80.

Even Ina Garten, the patron saint of Hamptons entertaining, is skeptical of a pie that costs that much.

“Unless it’s filled with lobster and caviar, I don’t understand it,” she said in a recent interview about holiday pie. “But then, I’ve also never tried one.”

Ms. Kristy, like others who are driving the new pie economy, says it’s time to hold pie in the same regard as elegant French tarts, whose premium prices don’t come under fire.

“If it tastes just as good and looks just as beautiful, it should be valued just the same,” said Ms. Kristy, who studied cooking in San Francisco and business at Columbia, and worked as a consumer brands consultant at McKinsey before turning her attention to jam in 2024.

“I feel really good about the quality of our pies,” she said. “This is a specialty item that is something you enjoy together with friends and there’s, like, a real thought behind it.”

To those who view pie as a denizen of the diner and the gift of grandmothers, luxury pie is an abomination.

“Pie should be accessible and affordable,” said Beth M. Howard, the Iowa baker and author whose 2025 documentary, “Pieowa: A Piece of America,” will premiere on PBS on Nov. 23. “The pioneers made pie, right? It’s a thing that is supposed to be homemade. If it becomes too fancy then, to me, it loses the magic.”

What makes a pie valuable, she said, isn’t smoked honey or handcrafted apple jam or a crust infused with British Cheddar. It’s time.

“The value goes up exponentially when you bring a homemade pie versus the pie you got with whatever cash you dropped at the bakery,” she said.

Joanie Spencer, who is editor in chief of Commercial Baking magazine and works with the American Pie Council, sees pie as a reflection of the K-shaped economy. Although most Thanksgiving hosts still make their own pie — albeit with some store-bought ingredients — others will happily pay a lot for a pie made by a pastry chef who uses premium ingredients. For still others, a $5.99 pumpkin pie from Costco that can feed 12 is a treat. (The company says it sold about nine million in 2024.)

Ms. Spencer points to research showing that many consumers these days are spending on special food items because they can’t afford bigger luxuries.

“There are people who might be, like, I can’t afford a car, but I have $135 so I’ll go buy this fancy pie and take it to my family’s house and have a special feeling, a special moment,” she said. “In the grand scheme of things, it’s not that much of an increase in their spending on food, and it feels special.”

The luxification of pie is not just a big-city phenomenon. The Goode Co., a Texas bakery that has been making pecan pies for 50 years, has partnered with a Houston jeweler this Thanksgiving. For $70, the company will send you a pecan pie in a special pine box. Of the thousands of pies the company expects to ship this season, 10 will have a golden ticket redeemable for a diamond bracelet.

In Missouri, expensive pie is not a new thing. The Blue Owl Bakery’s Levee High Apple Pie, whose towering dome is coated in pecan-studded caramel glaze, has been commanding high prices for years. It costs $130 if you order it from the food-delivery website Goldbelly, or $69 at the restaurant in Kimmswick, south of St. Louis.

Mary Hostetter and her daughter, Kim Byerly, created the pie to honor the volunteers who constructed a 10-foot levee to save the historic Mississippi River town from a flood in 1993. It’s a big seller at Thanksgiving, said Ms. Byerly’s husband, Dan, who defended the pie’s cost.

“There’s 18 apples in each pie, so it’s a huge pie,” he said. “And it’s made from scratch.”

Thanksgiving aside, people have been losing interest in pie, said Ms. Kogan, the Queens baker whose $150 pie will be available Thursday, when she opens Mishie’s Sunnyside, her bakery in Queens.

That’s in part why she turned her attention to pie. “I’ve been in this industry for 20 years,” said Ms. Kogan, a French Culinary Institute graduate who worked at several notable New York City restaurants before she opened a pie pop-up in Sunnyside, Queens, last year. “I just kind of saw this need to make a really American dessert like pie popular.”

A pie like hers requires several separate preparations. Quality ingredients are expensive. So are city rents and the cost of labor. Her prices range from $35 for a seven-inch pie to the 12-inch model for $150. “If you really break down the numbers, it’s not that crazy,” she said.

Ms. Howard, who once ran a pie shop in the Iowa house depicted in Grant Wood’s painting “American Gothic,” is not convinced that your Thanksgiving table needs a pricey pie.

“Pie’s been around a very, very long time, so why do we have to complicate it like we’re doing with everything else in the world?” she said. “Let’s just keep one thing sacred.”

item.title: This Trader Raised Alarm About Nvidia’s China Entanglements Months Ago
item.description:
Early on May 13, Christian Lamarco, a little-known stock researcher and trader, could barely sleep. Shortly after dawn the 31-year-old would release what amounted to the magnum opus of his career: A 40-page exposé on questionable behavior at Nvidia.

The report mostly comprised a sober examination of whether the chipmaker was being honest about the scale of its China business. But at the top of Page 3, Mr. Lamarco tucked in a paragraph-long warning of the “uncomfortably close relationship” between Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, and Alice Huang, who worked for Megaspeed, a huge customer.

Mr. Lamarco says his interest in their relationship had been piqued by reporting in The New York Times and Bloomberg News that first detailed a year ago how the Nvidia chief executive and Ms. Huang were seen together socializing with other tech executives in Asia.

So Mr. Lamarco started digging around for himself, using paid expert networks — middlemen that connect investors with company insiders — to chat with current and former Megaspeed and Nvidia employees about Ms. Huang and the companies’ business. The employees wondered about what Mr. Lamarco months ago termed “special” ties between the two executives.

But almost no one noticed his report.

Nvidia’s stock rose that day in May when Mr. Lamarco’s findings were released online. Among the little feedback, he recalled this week, was one note calling him developmentally disabled and another warning him to “watch out.”

Now, the 31-year-old looks prescient. On Thursday, Mr. Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO, after confessing to an extramarital affair with Ms. Huang, who U.S. intelligence has accused of being a Chinese spy.

(China rejects the espionage claims. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment, and Nvidia spokesmen did not respond to requests for comment.)

Nvidia’s once-soaring shares have fallen 24 percent over the past six months, including a 10 percent drop this week after the company’s board said it was investigating the matter.

“Everyone was just mocking us and now everyone is singing our praises,” Mr. Lamarco, who runs Culper Research, named after a Revolutionary War-era spy network, said in an interview.

Mr. Lamarco’s three-person New York firm is what is known as an activist short seller, or a trading shop that tries to convince other investors that a company’s shares will fall. The firm itself also wagers money that the stock will fall; the bigger the decline, the more money it makes.

Mr. Lamarco won’t say how much he’s earned off Nvidia trades, though this son of an upstate New York pastor is reticent to cloak his research on the company in any higher meaning.

“Short sellers get sanctimonious about this but it’s like, dude, you made $20 million last year. Don’t tell me you’re doing this as a public good,” Mr. Lamarco says.

Mr. Lamarco formed his firm in 2019, initially naming it Shadyside, after a neighborhood in Pittsburgh where he was living. Before taking on Nvidia, he had spent years investigating would-be scams, pump-and-dumps and just plain old overvalued companies to scant attention.

His initial targets could be described as small and getting smaller, such as LifeMD, a telehealth company whose stock dropped from $21 in 2021 just before he published his research note to less than $2 within a year.

Short sellers are not exactly popular on Wall Street, where many investors prefer to ride the rising, unimpeded tide of higher markets. The companies they target often complain that the reports are biased, overwrought or misleading.

Mr. Lamarco’s work has attracted its share of negative attention. He says he’s been repeatedly trailed by private investigators.

After he accused Tecnoglass, a window manufacturer, of having ties to the Sinaloa drug cartel, the company denied that accusation and sued for defamation in a lawsuit that said he had “no discernible, substantial real world experience to speak of.” Mr. Lamarco’s lawyers are seeking to have the suit dismissed.

Before publishing his research on Nvidia and Megaspeed, Mr. Lamarco didn’t run his findings by either company. These include his contention that, despite Nvidia’s claim that its business in China evaporated as a result of President Trump’s trade wars, in reality more than 20 percent of the company’s “compute revenue” could be traced there.

His analyses notwithstanding, Mr. Lamarco casts himself as anything but a Wall Street loudmouth. One friend described him as “pretty earnest.” In interviews, he’s so soft-spoken it’s almost tough to catch his words.

Mr. Lamarco says he was an unremarkable student at Grove City College, a Pennsylvania religious school, where he dabbled in posting to the financial website ZeroHedge. Asked if he enjoyed any hobbies, he says tennis, but hastens to add that he’s not very good.

Mr. Lamarco’s most surprising take at present might just be a measure of optimism for the chipmaker and its beleaguered chief executive.

“We’re not necessarily saying that Nvidia is going to zero or Jensen is going to end up in prison,” he says.

What will happen, then?

“That’s above my pay grade,” he says.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

]]>

item.title: Help! A Broken Toilet Grounded My Plane, and the Airline Won’t Cover a Hotel.
item.description:
On May 30, my wife and I were scheduled to take Turkish Airlines’ evening flight from Denver to Istanbul. The flight was delayed several hours because of what we were told was a mechanical problem. We boarded the aircraft at around 11:30 p.m., taxied to the runway and then returned to the gate. The flight was finally canceled at around 1 a.m. Gate agents advised us that no hotel vouchers were available and that we should find hotels and submit our receipts to the airline. We stayed at the airport Westin, paying $512, including taxes and breakfast, and flew out the next day. We heard — and later read in The Denver Post — that the cancellation had been caused by an overflowing lavatory. But the airline sent us a message attributing the disruption to “force majeure,” which to me means an earthquake or a war or something similar. I called the airline and was told to submit my hotel receipts online, which I did twice, but got no response. Turkish Airlines’ customer service plan says the carrier pays for hotels only if the reason for the cancellation was under its control. Is Turkish evading responsibility with this “force majeure” argument? Can you help? Neal, Broomfield, Colo.

How an airline describes the cause of a cancellation can directly affect whether it will cover passengers’ lodging, transportation and meals. For mechanical issues, the answer is often yes; for weather or air-traffic issues, it’s almost always no.

U.S. regulations define those categories, but they do not require airlines to pay for stranded passengers’ expenses. Nevertheless, all the major U.S. carriers except Frontier explicitly promise hotel stays in their customer service plans if the reason for the disruption is under their control. The Turkish Airlines policy for U.S. flights is a bit looser — but the airline usually offers lodging for controllable disruptions.

For the last couple of years, I’ve kept a file of emails from travelers who suspected, as you do, that a carrier had weaseled its way out of covering passengers’ expenses by misrepresenting what happened.

I had avoided the ever-expanding file because I knew that proving the precise cause of any one incident was most likely a fool’s errand. Disruptions can have multiple causes, and the U.S. Department of Transportation gives the airlines flexibility in determining the main one. For example, if a mechanical problem causes a delay, then a storm moves in and shuts down the airport, airlines can blame the weather. No hotel voucher for you!

But the evidence in your case seemed pretty overwhelming. When airlines cite force majeure, they are generally referring to extraordinary circumstances beyond their control — like a natural disaster. The Denver Post article had the headline “Turkish Airlines Cancels Flight From Denver Airport After Urine and Feces Erupt From Plane’s Toilet,” which is disgusting but hardly earthquake-level terrible. Citing force majeure seemed like, at best, an entertaining error or, at worst, an attempt to avoid compensating passengers for their hotels, a promise you said gate agents made at the time.

(I did also check if there were any earthquakes, floods or hostilities in either Colorado or Turkey around that time, and there were not.)

Armed with this information, I contacted Turkish Airlines about your flight. I got no response to my email (or to two follow-ups), but about a week after my first message, the airline sent you a message confirming the cause for the cancellation was the lavatory issue and sending a link to fill out a reimbursement form. You did so, and a month after that got your $512 back.

But since I had already begun to dig into my file, I didn’t stop with Turkish, choosing three more complaints — about United Airlines, Delta Air Lines and American Airlines — to pursue. Unfortunately, I had far less success with them.

Edna from El Portal, Fla., wrote in about a United Newark-to-Miami flight in July 2025 that was delayed after a plane had mechanical issues. The airline had found a replacement aircraft, she said, yet the flight was eventually canceled anyway. United categorized the disruption as weather-related and did not reimburse her $457 for a hotel and meals.

A spokeswoman for United, Stella Balaskas, noted that there were storms on the East Coast that day, which explained why the replacement plane could not fly. (Historical weather maps show storms between the two cities, though not in what seems to be the most common flight path between them.)

Chelsea of Pike Road, Ala., wrote to complain about an overnight delay as she returned from an anniversary trip to Maine with her husband in May 2025. After they boarded what would have been the final leg — a short nighttime hop from Atlanta to Montgomery, Ala. — the pilot announced that the flight had been delayed, overnight it turned out, because of an equipment problem in Montgomery. Delta agents blamed the weather and refused to provide hotels. Chelsea and her husband took a $145 Uber ride home and wanted to be reimbursed.

A Delta spokesman, Drake Castañeda, emailed me a statement noting that the delay had occurred “because the automated weather observing system at the Montgomery airport was intermittently unavailable.” So though it wasn’t exactly a weather issue, it was an airport issue, which would also exempt Delta from responsibility.

Finally, Mike of Poughkeepsie, N.Y., wrote that he spent $406 in hotel and other expenses when American canceled his flight in September from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport to Westchester County Airport, in New York. The first message he received about the delay implied it was maintenance-related, but American officially blamed air-traffic issues. Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for American, said that air-traffic constraints were the main reason for the cancellation. Again, no reimbursement.

As if all this weren’t frustrating enough, things are about to get worse for travelers. Next year, the federal government is planning to enact new rules that will add a category for cancellations outside an airline’s control, including designations like “unscheduled maintenance,” among others. This change will free the airlines from taking responsibility in a set of new circumstances. Will that include “unscheduled” broken airplane toilets? Maybe so.

The government’s notes about the rule change explicitly state that it will save the airlines money, which is another way of saying it will cost travelers money.

If you need advice about a best-laid travel plan that went awry, send an email to TrippedUp@nytimes.com.

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.

]]>

item.title: Voters Rejected Data Centers. Many Will Be Built Anyway.
item.description:
Many of the largest technology companies weren’t prepared for the opposition to data centers that has swept the country over the last year. To placate critics, the companies walked back secrecy arrangements, offered greater benefits to local communities and said they would pay more for electricity.

It didn’t matter. Even elected officials who had once welcomed the giant data centers, which tech companies are building for their artificial intelligence work, were turning against them. The election swung harder against data centers than polls predicted. In 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives across the country, citizens voted to limit or prevent data center development.

Still there are early signs that the Blue Wave that brought Democrats to power around the country will not send data center construction — and with it the U.S. economy — off a cliff.

One analysis, from the investment bank Bernstein, estimated that in the most extreme scenario, 9 percent of projects that would have probably been built will no longer break ground. More realistically, they said, only 2 to 4 percent of future data centers will be canceled nationwide.

Another analysis, from Susquehanna Financial Group, predicted that even if some projects die, more data centers for training A.I. will still be built in 2027 and 2028 than this year.

“We are not going to see a dramatic downturn,” said Austin Keyser, a top regional official at the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers who advised Amy Acton, Ohio’s Democratic governor-elect. She campaigned on establishing moratoriums on data center projects that don’t meet certain criteria, such as hiring union workers and building on former industrial sites, not farmland.

The Data Center Coalition, the leading industry trade group whose members include Amazon, Google and Microsoft, did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

The election results showed a lack of trust between the tech industry and local communities that will lead to a reset of how technology companies approach data center projects.

“I think we will look back at it for a positive thing in terms of setting more clear regulations and hopefully that will help communities feel we are not just in the Wild West here,” said Brian Janous, a former Microsoft executive who co-founded Cloverleaf Infrastructure, which puts together land and power deals for data center developers that work with OpenAI, Meta and others.

A large number of projects have permits and are under construction or will be soon, and elected officials haven’t generally proposed rescinding existing permits. Already there are more projects than the industry can realistically build. Shortages in labor, equipment and even power have already led to delays. Even before the election, the industry expected many announced deals to never pan out in the first place.

New rules could slow down projects, and force companies to pay more. But many of the biggest tech companies have already begun making the kinds of changes that people want. “Money is not their problem,” Mr. Keyser said. “If there is an impediment to them getting to market fast, they will pay their way through that.”

A gentle slowdown would be welcomed by some investors, who have become increasingly anxious as tech companies burn through cash to fuel their A.I. ambitions. Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta are on track to spend more than $720 billion this year on data centers and other capital expenses — roughly triple what they spent just two years ago.

Analysts and industry participants expect the largest, most established players have the resources and relationships to navigate the changes to come out ahead. Some have already been preparing for major changes and have been looking for ways to keep the boom alive.

Microsoft, for example, this summer ran polls in nine states where it has current or future operations, according to a person familiar with the company’s efforts. It found that while nothing would satisfy roughly 15 percent of people who oppose data centers, roughly 70 percent said could accept the buildings with protections, like generating tax revenue and limiting water use.

After realizing that it could not resolve opposition at the local level alone, Microsoft began drafting model legislation that it would bring to statehouses hungry to pass bills, the person said.

The smattering of issues that could be addressed with more Democrats in charge include rolling back tax breaks, requiring union labor, making data centers pay more for power, and being more transparent.

“The devil really is in the details on how do you a protect a community,” said Mandy DeRoche, who heads data center work at Earthjustice, an environmental nonprofit that has sued over certain projects. She said did not expect data center construction to come to a halt, but hoped that taking the edge off the frenzy could lead to better long-term thinking. Her group is particularly concerned about the growing reliance on natural gas to power A.I. data centers.

While the analysis from Susquehanna predicted that big tech companies can deal with the changes at the state and local level, smaller data center builders may not be so lucky.

These newer companies, called neoclouds, have taken on more debt than the industry giants, and could be more vulnerable to a pullback. Even before the election, many in the industry had expected neoclouds to consolidate. Gartner, a technology research firm, recently predicted that 80 percent of neoclouds will not be financially independent by 2030.

Some neoclouds have had to pay dearly to borrow enough money, and not all have been able to consistently deliver. Extra delays or costs could be harder to bear. “It will further separate the wheat from the chaff,” Mr. Janous said.

CoreWeave, a bellwether neocloud, had been punished by investors this year and forced to pay more to borrow. Its shares sank further right after the election. But on Tuesday it reported better than expected results in the quarter that ended Sept. 30.

Michael Intrator, CoreWeave’s chief executive, told investors it had strong demand for at least two years. And he made the case that the prices it can command may stay higher for longer because “if data center construction across the sector were to slow, installed compute becomes scarcer.” CoreWeave’s shares surged on Wednesday.

Still, there are many open questions, especially in Texas, where more data centers are planned than anywhere else in the country. Bernstein estimated that data center construction accounts for 28 percent of the state’s gross domestic product.

New permits in Texas were temporarily paused before the election pending an audit. But the campaign by Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic governor-elect, centered on establishing a moratorium on new data centers until the legislature passed protection on issues including reducing subsidies, using union labor, and banning nondisclosure agreements.

She told The New York Times in an interview that she did not think she could halt all the projects under construction, but that if they still needed approvals, she would “make sure those permits are held until we can protect Texans.” She said she was still pro-business — if the businesses were pro-Texas.

What exactly that means is not clear. Tech companies and developers are scrutinizing the status of their projects and wondering if they have all the permits they need or whether they could be caught up in the moratorium.

Constituents will be watching as new lawmakers juggle the risks of pulling the plug on economically important projects with what they promised on the campaign trail.

“That is why people voted,” Ms. DeRoche said.

item.title: Nvidia Shares Plunge, Shaking Up Tech Stocks
item.description:
Nvidia’s shares continued to slide on Thursday, sending tremors through global markets, as the company’s board considered the future of the chip-maker’s chief executive, Jensen Huang.

Shares in Nvidia dropped more than 7 percent in premarket trading, extending a drop that is set to wipe roughly $1 trillion from the company’s market value this month alone.

With the leadership of Nvidia in turmoil, investors faced uncertainty about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade and how the problems inside one of the technology industry’s most important companies could affect the broader economy.

The fallout could be seen in markets around the world, although the effects appeared limited. Major market indexes in Asia, where many of Nvidia’s partners and rivals in the artificial intelligence industry are based, mostly declined. Taiwan’s TSMC, which produces chips designed by Nvidia, fell more than 2 percent. But South Korea’s Samsung, which competes with Nvidia on some business lines, gained 1 percent.

European stock indexes, which have less heavy exposure to A.I., mostly rose on Thursday. But shares in the region’s largest tech company, ASML of the Netherlands, fell more than 2 percent.

In the United States, futures for the tech-heavy Nasdaq slipped less than 1 percent in premarket trading. The stocks of Nvidia’s fellow tech giants, members of an exclusive club known as the “Magnificent Seven,” were little changed.

Shares in some of Nvidia’s U.S. chip-making rivals were set to climb: AMD rose more than 2 percent and Broadcom gained nearly 2 percent in premarket trading on Thursday. The broader S&P 500 was set to open slightly lower.

Trading outside of official market hours is often choppy, which can exaggerate moves in stock prices.

Mr. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has become one of the most influential forces in the A.I. boom, which has helped to drive U.S. stock markets to new highs in recent years.

Nvidia’s board deliberations came after revelations that Mr. Huang had an affair with an executive who reports to him as well as with a woman whom U.S. intelligence has identified as a Chinese spy.

Some market analysts covering Nvidia have begun to downgrade their forecasts for the company’s stock. Though the chipmaker is expected to remain a critical part of the A.I. build-out, some noted rising concerns about the company’s governance and lack of a clear succession plan. They argued that these revelations have fundamentally changed Mr. Huang’s position in the tech world and its unclear what the implications of a change in his role at Nvidia could be.

Analysts at Bernstein downgraded Nvidia and sharply lowered their target for its share price. “Our gut tells us that we probably haven’t yet fully probed the depths of what might be found here,” they wrote. “We’ve had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines.”

Analysts at RBC Capital Markets also slashed their forecast for the stock, citing the lack of formal succession plan for the chief executive position. “Whether any individual can replicate Huang’s singular combination of technical vision, ecosystem-building acumen, and ability to serve as the global face of the A.I. revolution remains an open question,” they noted.

Other analysts, including those at Wells Fargo and Mizuho, maintained their bullish views on Nvidia, but said it was increasingly likely that Mr. Huang may not be chief executive for much longer.

Nvidia’s stock is down about a third from its peak at the start of October, putting the company deep in a bear market, defined as a drop of 20 percent or more from a recent high.

Nvidia became the world’s largest public company, by market value, for the first time in 2024, exerting an outsize influence over major indexes like the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500. Analysts still expect Nvidia to make a profit of well over $200 billion this year, with its chips in high demand as tech companies rush to build giant A.I. data centers.

During last week’s market turmoil, Nvidia fell below Apple as the world’s biggest public company.

item.title: Imagining Nvidia Without Jensen Huang
item.description:
Andrew here. Put yourself in the shoes of Nvidia’s board: Would you fire Jensen Huang?

An affair with a customer who U.S. intelligence officials determined was a spy for China, as well as what The Times reported was a relationship with an employee, would typically be grounds for removal. At best, these scandals are a distraction. At worst, they make managing the nearly $4 trillion chipmaker virtually impossible, especially if credible evidence emerges that Huang knew about Nvidia chips improperly going to China.

Yet does his centrality to the company and the A.I. industry mean overlooking those issues? Elon Musk wrote that he would be honored to hire Huang. Palmer Luckey of Anduril declared, “China wants Jensen out, so I want him in.” The venture capitalist Sarah Guo wrote, “We should demand loyalty and accountability, but sainthood cannot be the price of admission to leadership.”

Does the Nvidia board have any middle ground? Could Huang step down to become chief technology officer — or is that just window dressing? We should know the answer soon. More below.

A month ago, Jensen Huang was firmly ensconced atop Nvidia. Now Silicon Valley — and Wall Street and Washington — are starting to imagine life without him running the giant chipmaker.

If Nvidia’s board removes Huang as C.E.O., it would be a sea change at the central cog of the artificial intelligence boom, with wide-ranging consequences, Sri Muppidi and Michael de la Merced report.

The latest:

Nvidia’s board has met to discuss Huang’s future, after The Times reported that he had an affair with a direct report, Kimberly Powell, as well as with Alice Huang, an executive who U.S. intelligence officials determined is a spy for China. (The Wall Street Journal suggests that his ouster is on the table.)

Alice Huang is now living in Beijing, with the knowledge of Chinese security officials, Bloomberg reports, citing unnamed sources.

What Nvidia without Huang as C.E.O. might look like: Remember that the company has no clear succession plan. Analysts have speculated that Colette Kress, its C.F.O. and perhaps its next most prominent executive, could become interim C.E.O. (Nvidia has hired an outside firm to consider possible replacements for Huang, according to Bloomberg, which cited unnamed sources.)

But no one at the company possesses the depth of operational knowledge or the authority of Huang, who has roughly 60 direct reports. Names floated among Nvidia watchers as possible outside candidates include Lisa Su of AMD, Rene Haas of Arm Holdings, Lip-Bu Tan of Intel and Johny Srouji of Apple.

Any disruption at Nvidia could shake up the tech industry. The company’s processors, known as GPUs, underpin a vast majority of A.I. data centers, including most run by SpaceX, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, SoftBank, CoreWeave and others.

“SpaceX has committed to using Nvidia GPUs exclusively because they are the best,” Elon Musk wrote on social media in August.

Analysts have asked whether customers would start canceling orders: “A lot of these A.I. purchasing decisions are done by the C.E.O.s at the top, and now the person shaking those hands is no longer there,” Brian Colello, a senior analyst at Morningstar, told DealBook.

But even some competitors said that Nvidia’s moat — including its CUDA software platform that is used by much of the A.I. world — remains formidable. “Those things don’t disappear because of things in the personal life of the C.E.O.,” Bernardo Kastrup, a founder and C.E.O. of Euclyd, a start-up designer of chips that compete with Nvidia’s, told DealBook on Tuesday.

What about Nvidia’s role as the central banker of the A.I. economy? Nvidia’s stock is down nearly 8 percent in premarket trading, and more than 13 percent over the past five days. Several analysts cut their ratings for Nvidia, or at least their price targets, including at Baird, Morgan Stanley and Citi.

One big question: What would happen to the billions of dollars in financial guarantees and backstops that Nvidia has offered to so-called neoclouds and start-ups to undergird the A.I. boom?

What about the influence vacuum in Washington? Huang, along with Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, has been one of the most prominent voices in President Trump’s ear on A.I. policy. Some A.I. leaders, including Sam Altman of OpenAI, have privately vented that Huang was perhaps too influential in pushing for a lighter touch on regulation.

If Huang is ousted, A.I. executives, including Altman, Musk and Zuckerberg, would almost surely rush to assume his role as chief “Trump whisperer” on the topic.

Nvidia’s problem is that no internal C.E.O. candidate would have the same sway as Huang, a potential issue when it comes to pushing for permission to sell more chips to China. The mood in Washington (and in much of the White House) has shifted to being tougher on China — with apparent holdouts like Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick facing more heat.

Mississippi elects a Democrat, Scott Colom, to the U.S. Senate. Colom will be the first Black person to represent Mississippi in the chamber since the Reconstruction era. (His backers include George and Alex Soros, the Democratic donors.) Colom defeated the state’s incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican, in a major political upset that is expected to give Democrats a sizable legislative advantage in Washington starting next year.

United Airlines is banning third-party artificial intelligence agents from booking flights. The airline said the tools could expose sensitive customer information or make unintended purchases if agents are able to gain access to its ticketing systems. Companies are grappling with whether to permit outside agents to peruse and buy amid concerns that the technology might upend their relationship with customers and pricing power. United’s biggest domestic rivals, Delta Air Lines and American Airlines, have adopted more permissive policies about allowing agents for booking.

A closely watched sexual harassment case against SpaceX advances. A federal appeals court denied an attempt by Elon Musk’s company to shift a lawsuit, which was brought by eight former employees, to private arbitration. (The employees were fired after they wrote a letter urging the company to distance itself from comments Musk made, including one poking fun at sexual harassment accusations against him.) Elsewhere, a growing number of young people are suing SpaceX’s A.I. division, arguing that its Grok model was used to create sexualized images of them as children.

Artificial intelligence bulls have received a lift this week from a battered corner of the market: the so-called neoclouds. Market watchers are already wondering how long it will last.

Shares of two of the biggest ones — CoreWeave and Nebius — rallied impressively on Wednesday. Both companies are major Nvidia customers, and they lease computing power to A.I. labs.

Shares in both companies are down sharply in premarket trading. Nebius this morning reported a big jump in revenue last quarter.

The bull case: CoreWeave delivered blowout third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, and raised its full-year revenue projection on the back of heavy demand. Michael Intrator, the company’s C.E.O., said computing demand was “oversubscribed” for the next two years

The bear case: CoreWeave needs huge amounts of capital. Until now it has relied mostly on riskier “junk” bonds, which often carry high interest rates, to finance its buildout. But the cost of borrowing has been rising, prompting investors to worry about its ability to pay back the debt and still grow.

Now CoreWeave is reportedly preparing to tap the credit market again. It plans to raise at least $4 billion through investment-grade bonds, Bloomberg reports:

Morgan Stanley and Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group Inc. are leading the potential financing, which would be syndicated to investors in phases, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The deal may come to market as soon as next week, but the plans haven’t been finalized and could change, the people said, asking not to be identified because they’re not authorized to speak publicly.

The junk-rated company has been heavily reliant on the high-yield debt markets to finance its buildout, but has been able to lock in cheaper borrowing costs by using chips and related contracts to back its debt — a structure that is expected to be used for the new financing.

The bonds could be sold at a yield of 7 percent to 7.5 percent, according to Bloomberg, which is roughly half the yield of where its junk bonds are trading.

Quote of the day

Alex Karp, the C.E.O. of Palantir, a major government contractor, describing his political leanings to Politico after Democrats seized control of Congress in the midterm elections. Karp, who called the Democratic Party “totally irresponsible” last year and has donated to the MAGA Inc. super PAC, also told Politico that Republicans’ losses in this election cycle were a “referendum” on “economic justice.”

Tributes are pouring in for Judge Richard Posner, a giant of American jurisprudence and a prolific writer on economics and policy, who died on Tuesday. He was 87.

For nearly 40 years, Posner served on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, in Chicago. As Adam Liptak of The Times notes, his work included:

thousands of judicial opinions and more than 50 books on a vast array of topics, along with countless scholarly articles, essays, book reviews and blog posts.

He was, the journalist Gary Rosen wrote in The Wall Street Journal in 2002, “a one-man think tank.”

Posner was one of the most influential jurists of his generation. He was an author of legal opinions in numerous major business, antitrust and intellectual property cases.

As an author, Posner weighed on both meaty and quotidian topics, including counterterrorism, sex and the economics of college tuition.

An ardent defender of free markets, he stunned many with his 2009 book, “A Failure of Capitalism: The Crisis of ’08 and the Descent into Depression.” In it, he laid the blame for the global financial crisis of that era more squarely on the capitalist system itself than on Washington or Wall Street.

What people have said about Posner:

“He taught me to think without fear,” Tim Wu, a professor at Columbia Law School who clerked for Posner and later advised Joe Biden on competition and antitrust policies, wrote on social media.

“He was one of the rare people who ever change their minds,” Richard Thaler, the economist and Nobel laureate, wrote on social media. “At first he knew behavioral economics was wrong, but he softened over time.”

“One of the most brilliant, hard-working and intellectually honest people I have ever met,” wrote Luis Garicano, a Spanish economist and professor at the London School of Economics, who worked with Posner to analyze U.S. intelligence failures after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. “He wrote his own opinions rather than leaving them to his clerks.”

Deals

iHeartMedia is said to be considering a sale of all or some of its podcast business in an effort to raise cash and prop up its flagging share price. (Bloomberg)

Agile Robots, a robotics start-up, has raised $500 million in funding from investors including SoftBank and Nvidia that values it at $8.5 billion. (NYT)

Politics, policy and regulation

Gavin de Becker, a campaign donor and security consultant, reportedly funded part of one of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s summer vacations, including a yacht trip in Greece. (WSJ)

Voters rejected data centers in the midterm elections. Many will be built anyway. (NYT)

Best of the rest

“Humans cause most accidents. Is Grand Theft Auto the key to safer roads?” (BBC)

Gen Z is doing its part to bolster the movie industry as it flocks to art houses, silent film series and obscure international flicks. (NYT)

We’d like your feedback! Please email thoughts and suggestions to dealbook@nytimes.com.

]]>

item.title: Singapore Says U.S. Not Helpful on Investigation Into Suspected Spy’s Company
item.description:
Singapore’s government said on Thursday the United States had provided little help in its investigation into Alice Huang, the woman at the center of a spy plot that has led to the investigation of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang.

Singaporean authorities held Ms. Huang’s passport to prevent her from leaving the country from June 2025 until February over “potential false declarations” in relation to her company, Megaspeed, which is based in the country, the government said in a statement. She was ultimately released with a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore.

The statement raises new questions about the response of the Trump administration to the case and why the U.S. government did not more forcefully intervene. According to the timeline in the statement, Singaporean authorities had been holding Ms. Huang’s passport well after President Trump was briefed last fall about her relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive and the belief that she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

The New York Times has reported that Taiwan began monitoring Ms. Huang in 2024 at the guidance of the U.S. government.

In its statement, Singapore said that it had sought information from an American server maker and close Nvidia business partner, Supermicro, but that the company had been uncooperative. Supermicro, a firm that packages Nvidia’s A.I. chips onto servers that can be used in data centers, has been at the center of a number of chip smuggling investigations across the globe.

Supermicro was a supplier to Megaspeed, a company incorporated in Singapore and run by Ms. Huang, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.

Singapore said in the statement its authorities raised Supermicro’s “limited cooperation” with the U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation in July 2025 and “requested their assistance in securing the company’s cooperation.”

“Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” the statement said.

Supermicro did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

During questioning, Ms. Huang sought to downplay her role in Megaspeed, according to Singapore’s statement. She was ultimately released because of “insufficient evidence relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated.”

She was issued a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore. The country’s police are continuing to investigate Megaspeed.

item.title: Here’s the latest.
item.description:
Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the Silicon Valley chip giant Nvidia, resigned on Thursday, according to the company’s board of directors, capping a swift, stunning fall for one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom. His departure came after revelations that he had extramarital affairs with an executive who reported to him and with a woman whom U.S. intelligence agencies concluded was spying for China.

Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive while the search for a permanent replacement is carried out, Nvidia’s 10-member board said in a statement. In a note to Nvidia employees, Ms. Kress said she believes “deeply in this company” and called its employees “our greatest strength.”

Mr. Huang’s exit, which followed a lengthy board meeting on Wednesday, opens an uncertain chapter for Nvidia, the premier maker of artificial intelligence chips, and will have widespread ripple effects. Its shares plunged at the start of trading, weighing on the broader market.

Over three decades, Mr. Huang, 63, built Nvidia into one of the world’s most valuable public companies, controlling an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips that are an essential component of the artificial intelligence projects driving the U.S. economy — and are at the center of the U.S.-China tussle for dominance in A.I.

A series of reports by The New York Times showed that Mr. Huang had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who goes by Alice Huang, who had been recruited by China’s main spy agency to gather information on Mr. Huang, and that President Trump had been warned about the relationship but took no action.

U.S. officials suspect that Megaspeed, the Singaporean company where Ms. Huang was a top executive, has helped smuggle restricted chips into China. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment, and China has rejected the espionage claims and called the smuggling allegations “smears.”

Nvidia’s board, which has had a long track record of deference to its celebrity C.E.O., did not mention Mr. Huang’s conduct in its statement. It called his contributions to Nvidia “profound” and thanked him for his “immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.”

Here’s what else to know:

A second affair: Mr. Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an executive who reported to him, according to five people who worked at the company, The Times reported on Wednesday. Under Nvidia’s code of conduct, employees are told to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships,” and the company states that it “promptly investigates reports of misconduct.” Read more ›

Economic fallout: Mr. Huang’s departure could affect the economy more broadly than a typical C.E.O. departure. He ran Nvidia almost single-handedly and was unusually central its success. Nvidia, in turn, has been unusually central to the artificial intelligence boom, a crucial driver of U.S. economic growth while some other sectors have been struggling. Read more ›

Huang and Trump: Few tech executives have has as much sway with Mr. Trump, who has called Mr. Huang an “honorable man” and said he believed that Mr. Huang was not aware he had been involved with a Chinese spy. The president is scheduled to travel to China next week, and he said on Monday that he did not plan to bring up the Nvidia matter in talks with China’s leader, Xi Jinping.

item.title: What to Know About Colette Kress, Nvidia’s New Interim Chief Executive
item.description:
Colette Kress, a longtime Nvidia executive, was appointed by the board of directors as the interim chief executive officer.

In a note to Nvidia employees on Thursday, Ms. Kress said she believes “deeply in this company” and each of its employees. “This company has achieved so much because of the work that all of you bring to it every single day,” she said.

Nvidia veteran: Ms. Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, joined Nvidia in 2013. She has worked closely with Mr. Huang as the company transitioned from a niche maker of graphics processors used for video games to a company at the center of the artificial intelligence boom. She previously worked for Cisco and Microsoft. She has an undergraduate degree in finance from the University of Arizona and a M.B.A. from Southern Methodist University. She will remain the company’s finance chief while serving as interim chief executive.

Closeness to Jensen Huang: Mr. Huang interviewed 22 candidates before hiring Ms. Kress as chief financial officer. At the time, Ms. Kress’s young sons, who were avid gamers, encouraged her to join Nvidia. During her first week on the job, Ms. Kress asked Mr. Huang how long he thought he would want her in the role. “I said, ‘For as long as we shall live and death do us part,’” Mr. Jensen said in a podcast appearance this year.

China: During her time as chief financial officer, Ms. Kress expressed concerns about the financial impact of American policies that restrict Nvidia sales to China. In 2023, she said on a call with financial analysts that China accounted for 20 to 25 percent of the company’s data center revenue. In addition to lost sales, she has said the policies risk strengthening Nvidia’s competitors in China.

Liaison to Wall Street: As chief financial officer, one of Ms. Kress’s main responsibilities was communicating with Wall Street and Nvidia’s investors. On quarterly earnings calls, Ms. Kress delivered a rosy message as Nvidia’s revenue and stock price soared. In 2013, Nvidia’s sales were $4.28 billion. In the most recent fiscal year, its annual sales reached $215.9 billion.

Personal Wealth: Ms. Kress has benefited from Nvidia’s skyrocketing stock price. She owned roughly 4.44 million shares, according to Nvidia’s most recent annual report, worth about $772 million.

item.title: A Timeline of Jensen Huang’s Affairs That Upended Nvidia
item.description:
News that Jensen Huang, the co-founder of Nvidia, was having an affair with a woman believed to be Chinese spy has sent shock waves through the tech world, the U.S. government and the wider economy.

Mr. Huang served as Nvidia’s chief executive from 1993, when he co-founded the company, until his resignation on Thursday. He rocketed to prominence during the A.I. boom as Nvidia’s advanced chips became a crucial technology, making it one of the world’s most valuable companies. Mr. Huang, 63, has close ties to President Trump and has frequently appeared alongside him.

Here’s how the events unfolded.

2023: A Chinese executive named Alice Huang sets up a data firm in Singapore called Megaspeed. The company, which originally had Chinese owners, would soon buy billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips. In May 2023, Nvidia reaches $1 trillion in value.

December 2023: While it’s not clear when Mr. Huang, who is married, met Ms. Huang, they were acquainted by December 2023, when they had dinner with colleagues at a restaurant in Singapore. In June 2024, they were seen socializing at an event in Taipei.

June 2024 to June 2025: A Megaspeed subsidiary receives more than 200 shipments of Nvidia A.I. equipment.

July 2025: Nvidia becomes the first public company ever to be worth $4 trillion.

September 2025: The U.S. government, through the Commerce Department, begins an investigation into Megaspeed, examining whether some of the Nvidia chips it bought were sent to China, a possible violation of U.S. export controls.

Early 2025: Weeks after Mr. Trump begins his second term, Mr. Huang visits the White House to meet with him for the first time.

March 2025: Ms. Huang visits Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif.

April 2025: During a dinner for donors at Mar-a-Lago, Mr. Huang makes a case to Mr. Trump for allowing chip companies like Nvidia to do business with China. The same month, the White House shuts down Nvidia’s sales to China, strengthening Biden-era regulations that put limits on the sale of A.I. technology.

May 2025: Ms. Huang and Mr. Huang dine with others in Taipei. They pose for a photo together, and she kisses him on the cheek.

July 2025: The Trump administration reverses course and assures Nvidia that it will be granted a license to sell certain chips to China.

October 2025: U.S. intelligence officials tell Mr. Trump that Mr. Huang has a relationship with Ms. Huang, who they describe as a Chinese intelligence asset. Mr. Trump chooses not to take any action.

December 2025: Mr. Trump approves the sale of more powerful Nvidia chips to China.

May 2026: Secretary of State Marco Rubio warns U.S. officials that Mr. Huang is in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. The same month, Mr. Trump invites Mr. Huang to join him on a state visit to Beijing.

October 2026: Mr. Huang’s affair with Ms. Huang is reported in The New York Times.

November 2026: After Mr. Huang admits the affair, Nvidia’s board says it will conduct an investigation. The New York Times later reports that Mr. Huang also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reports to him.

On Nov. 12, Nvidia’s board of directors announces that Mr. Huang has resigned.

item.title: Jensen Huang Was the Face of the A.I. Boom Powering the U.S. Economy
item.description:
It seems crazy to suggest that the downfall of one chief executive could have macroeconomic implications, but in this case it might be true.

Jensen Huang, as has been widely discussed in recent days, ran Nvidia almost single-handedly and was unusually central to his company’s success. Nvidia, in turn, has been unusually central to the artificial intelligence boom — not just developing the chips that run most A.I. models, but also helping to finance the data center build out.

And that build out has become a crucial driver of U.S. economic growth while some other sectors are struggling. Moreover, Mr. Huang’s ouster comes at what was already a delicate time for the A.I. industry. There have been signs in recent months that investors are growing more skeptical that companies will be able to deliver returns that justify the huge investments they are making in A.I., or at least that those returns could take longer than expected to materialize.

And Democrats’ sweeping victories in last week’s midterm elections could lead to new restrictions on data center construction, which could jeopardize the industry’s boom. In the past, when confidence in the A.I. story has wavered, Mr. Huang and Nvidia have often been the ones to calm doubts, reporting huge sales figures or stepping in to provide financing to data center projects whose future seemed in jeopardy.

This time around, it isn’t clear who will fill the void.

item.title: Jensen Huang Joins a Growing Club: C.E.O.s Brought Down by Affairs
item.description:
The “close personal relationship” has been the downfall of a number of chief executives over the years.

Now it has felled Jensen Huang, the founder and chief executive of Nvidia. Mr. Huang resigned on Thursday following revelations that he had an affair with an executive at the company as well as with a woman whom U.S. intelligence agencies concluded was an intelligence asset for China.

Posing a risk to national security is not the usual reason for ousting a chief executive. More often, it is that a relationship was in violation of company policy.

Large companies generally have had policies that prohibit managers and direct reports from having romantic relationships. Nvidia’s code of conduct tells employees to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships.”

“When it comes to direct reports, companies have had hard policies and have had for ages,” said Charles G. Tharp, executive vice president of the CHRO Association, a group for human resources officers.

Mr. Tharp added that companies likely tightened enforcement on these policies in the wake of the Me Too era.

Mark Hurd, who had helped build HP into a powerhouse tech company, was fired in 2010 after its board found that he’d failed to disclose use of company funds, and that he’d had a “close personal relationship” with a contractor. In 2018, Brian Krzanich resigned from Intel after the chip company learned of a “past consensual relationship” the chief executive had with an employee.

Tech is not the only industry to be hit by scandal. Last year, Ashley Buchanan was fired as chief executive of Kohl’s, the department store chain, after the company learned that he was trying to direct business to a vendor who turned out to be his romantic partner. Mr. Buchanan was in the role for just a few months. Rodney McMullen, the chief executive of the grocery chain Kroger, resigned last year after an investigation by its board found that his personal conduct was inconsistent with the company’s policies.

McDonald’s went through an unusually public yearslong battle starting in 2019. That year, the company fired Steve Easterbrook, its chief executive, after its board learned he had engaged in a consensual relationship with a subordinate that violated company policy. Eight months later, another McDonald’s employee reported a previous sexual relationship with Mr. Easterbrook. McDonald’s then sued Mr. Easterbrook, accusing him of lying and concealing multiple relationships with McDonald’s employees. The case was settled, and Mr. Easterbrook apologized and gave back more than $105 million in cash and stock to the company.

In 2018, Leslie Moonves, the longtime chief executive of the CBS Corporation, was one of the most high-profile entertainment figures to be ousted from his position during the #MeToo era. He stepped down after several women accused him of sexual harassment. Mr. Moonves received no severance package.

In the wake of Mr. Moonves’s ouster, the board of CBS also named six new members.

Boards of directors are responsible for monitoring the conduct of their chief executives and ultimately decide if a chief executive needs to step down.

Founders of very successful companies — like Mr. Huang — are often treated with deference by their boards. “They are in awe of their founder for very good reasons,” said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a professor of leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and the author of “The Hero’s Farewell.”

In Nvidia’s case, he said, “the board has done the right thing, but it has taken too long,”

“There were lots of indicators for any board paying attention,” he added.

Other founders have been fired because of their temperament or management style and later ended up returning to the companies they built. In 1985, Steve Jobs was forced out of Apple after an internal power struggle and a disastrous rollout of new technology. In 2000, he returned and had a legendary run as Apple’s chief executive. Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, had a shorter time away from his artificial-intelligence empire. He was pushed out by the board of directors on a Friday afternoon in 2023. Five days later, he was reinstated as the company’s leader after allies, including fellow Silicon Valley executives, employees and investors, urged his return.

item.title: Jensen Huang’s Ouster From Nvidia Could Complicate Billions in Philanthropic Giving
item.description:
Jensen Huang was just becoming one of America’s biggest philanthropists before his departure as the chief executive of Nvidia. With an estimated net worth of about $145 billion, he and his wife, Lori, had built one of the country’s largest foundations, with about $9 billion in assets.

But Mr. Huang said this week that he had been unfaithful to his wife, acknowledging an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence has determined was a Chinese spy. The Times then reported that he had another affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him. Nvidia said on Thursday morning that Mr. Huang was resigning from the company he had led for 33 years.

The fate of the foundation, which the couple started in 2007 and oversee together, is not clear.

Ms. Huang is the foundation’s president, and Mr. Huang is its secretary and chief financial officer, according to the most recent tax return for the charitable organization, which is called the Jen-hsun & Lori Huang Foundation. In 2024, its most recent tax year on file, the foundation’s assets nearly tripled, thanks to more than $5 billion in investment gains.

Marital issues have led to major shifts in the world of philanthropy in recent years, such as the departure from Melinda French Gates from her joint charitable entity with her ex-husband, Bill, and the elevation of MacKenzie Scott as one of America’s biggest givers following her divorce from Jeff Bezos.

The Huangs’s foundation is rather low-profile: Despite being one of America’s biggest charitable entities, it hosts no website or lists any public staff.

And the couple had only just begun their giving. The biggest public gifts by the Huangs have gone to higher-education institutions, a relatively safe and conventional place to disburse large amounts of money. They have announced a combined $180 million or so to four schools, including a $75 million donation in July to establish an art and design college at Vanderbilt University’s planned outpost in San Francisco.

Mr. Huang has described his philanthropic giving as an investment, not charity. “I don’t give anything away,” he said in 2010, dismissing the premise of the question. “The way I think about it is I’m investing in the next generation, to help us and to inspire us to create even better and more useful technologies.”

Their giving has also intersected with what is good for Nvidia. The Huangs’ foundation bought computing time from Coreweave, a key Nvidia partner and customer, and donated $108.3 million of it to universities and other nonprofits, according to an Nvidia corporate filing in May.

item.title: Mortgage Rates Remain High as Affordability Challenges Persist
item.description:
Mortgage rates slid for the fourth consecutive week but remain above 7 percent, adding pressure to a bleak housing market struggling with rising prices and declining sales.

The rate on the most popular home loan in the United States, the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage, fell slightly to 7.11 percent, from 7.18 percent the week before, the mortgage finance giant Freddie Mac said on Thursday. The same rate averaged 6.24 percent a year ago.

There was hope that mortgage rates might ease below 7 percent, a psychological threshold that could draw more buyers to the market. But industry experts say that marker is not likely to be breached any time soon.

High housing costs have made buying a home unaffordable for many Americans, said Brad Case, the chief residential economist at Homes.com, a real estate search portal owned by CoStar, a data analytics company.

“I don’t think affordability challenges are going away any time soon,” he added, “because I don’t think we’re likely to see substantially lower mortgage rates.”

Squeezed by high mortgage rates and rising inflation, buyers and sellers are sitting out of the market until conditions improve, which has depressed home sales. Sales of existing homes fell 8.8 percent in October from the year before, and 5.5 percent lower than September’s pace, according to a report released Thursday by the National Association of Realtors, a trade group.

Existing-home sales have fallen to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million, their slowest since August 2010, the NAR report said. A healthy annual sales pace is typically about five million existing homes.

“It’s a tough market for buyers and sellers,” Lawrence Yun, NAR’s chief economist, said Thursday on a call with reporters, adding that the sales outlook for 2026 is looking increasingly gloomy. “It could be one of the lowest annual figures, once we tally up the final three months of this year,” he said.

Affordability challenges are likely to keep sales low for the next few months, said Danielle Hale, chief economist at Realtor.com. a listings website.

“I don’t think this is a new normal for home sales,” she said in a statement. “Instead, it reflects a perfect storm of an abrupt shift in the financial environment and large uncertainties in the pre-election period for both policy and the economy just as the housing market usually slows for the season.”

The housing market began to lock up in 2022, when mortgage rates started to climb after falling below 3 percent. Homeowners who snagged the ultralow rates have been unwilling to sell, which has put the market in a prolonged gridlock.

“You are going to have a frozen housing market for a long time,” said Jeff Ostrowski, housing market analyst at Bankrate, a consumer financial services company. “It’s been, I think, even more dramatic than anyone expected, just because mortgage rates went up so much.”

Mortgage rates fell below 6 percent the last week of February, giving hope that the housing market might rebound, but they began rising again after the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28. The war, which has lasted more than eight months, has driven up costs for fuel and food.

Consumer prices rose sharply in October, climbing 0.4 percent after a 0.6 percent increase in September. But wage growth has not kept pace, and home buyers are feeling the pinch because they have less to put toward a home.

“For affordability to get better, what really needs to happen is income growth,” Mr. Case of Homes.com said.

The jump in inflation has increased the odds that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its next meeting in December, which could put upward pressure on mortgage rates. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which underpins consumer loans like mortgages, climbed above 5 percent after the inflation report was released on Tuesday.

item.title: Ask Us Anything About A.I. and Our Journalism
item.description:
Artificial intelligence is remaking the world. From music and science to the influencer economy and politics, no industry is immune to the influence of A.I. — and that includes journalism. What does that look like in The New York Times’s newsroom?

The Times has guiding principles for the use of A.I. in our journalism. In short, we use it carefully, with humans in charge. Our reporters have used A.I. to help comb through documents and large data sets, including the Epstein files and President Trump’s public speeches.

What questions do you have about how we use A.I.?

Ask about anything, and editors and reporters from across our newsroom will answer as many questions as possible. We will not publish any part of your submission without contacting you and hearing back, nor will we share your contact information outside our newsroom.
