item.title: Fed Will Not Hold Policy Vote at October 2027 Meeting
item.description:
The Federal Reserve announced a revised schedule for its policy meetings next year, scrapping a vote on interest rates in October and spacing out other gatherings such that officials will no longer meet in December. The changes are part of a broader plan Kevin M. Warsh, who took over as chairman of the central bank in May, has put in place to cut back on the number of meetings each year.

According to a revised 2027 schedule the Fed released on Thursday, officials will still meet eight times over the course of next year. But instead of discussing the near-term policy outlook, the Oct. 26-27 meeting will now be “dedicated to the discussion of broad monetary policy strategy issues.” A meeting in November was set for the middle of the month and without a December gathering, the Fed will not vote on rates again until it meets Jan. 25-26, 2028.

Mr. Warsh unveiled last month the broad contours of his plan, which by 2028 will involve the central bank reducing the number of rate-setting meetings to six and holding two strategy-focused meetings. The strategy meetings will not involve a policy vote and are not expected to be accompanied by a post-meeting statement.

“Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals,” Mr. Warsh said at a news conference in late October when explaining his decision. “But it’s equally important we reserve time and space, as an intellectually diverse group, for strategic deliberations — for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point.”

Mr. Warsh said the cadence of the Fed’s meetings was “more than some administrative detail.” Instead, he said it was an “institutional choice, affecting the nature and the quality of our deliberations and, ultimately, the wisdom of our decisions. It’s yet another change to get the conduct of monetary policy on the right track.”

One potential cost of the Fed meeting less frequently is that officials there will have fewer opportunities to adjust the central bank’s policy settings if the economic backdrop shifts. That raises the possibility the Fed will have to call impromptu meetings, which in the past have typically been reserved for crises.

In addition to changing how often the Fed meets, Mr. Warsh has vowed to overhaul the way the central bank communicates. He has already drastically shortened the policy statement that is published alongside each rate decision. His news conferences have been much more abridged than his predecessors’, and he has opted against submitting economic projections as part of a quarterly release of forecasts that policymakers have published for years.

Mr. Warsh’s rejection of the “dot plot” reflects his opposition to providing any guidance about the outlook, a practice that he argues has not only boxed in policymakers, but also disrupted important signals they would otherwise get from financial markets.

He has dedicated one of five task forces to look into how the Fed communicates, suggesting there could be significant changes to come.

item.title: SpaceX Plans $74 Billion Investment to Build Data Centers in Texas and Arizona
item.description:
SpaceX said on Thursday that it planned to invest $74 billion to build new data center campuses in Arizona and Texas as the company continued to pour money into the global artificial intelligence race.

The projects, proposed by Elon Musk’s rocket and A.I. company, would be among some of the largest data center projects in the United States.

In Texas, SpaceX plans to invest $24 billion in a data center campus on 444 acres of company-owned land near the Starbase rocket site in the Rio Grande Valley. The data center in Texas will generate its own power rather than rely on the public grid, the company said in its announcement. It is not immediately clear whether the project needs any further regulatory approvals.

In Arizona, SpaceX plans to build a $50 billion campus in Cochise County, which will create 5,500 construction jobs and 1,000 permanent jobs, the company said. The Arizona project still requires approval from the county.

SpaceX, which went public this year in the biggest initial public offering in history, has quickly grown its business leasing out computing power to other A.I. companies like Anthropic and Google. In October, SpaceX reported that its A.I. business accounted for more than half its revenue.

Anthropic has committed to paying up to $120.5 billion through 2029. Google is also paying SpaceX $920 million per month for computing power.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

SpaceX’s A.I. unit — xAI — has been at the forefront of the data center build out and operates four data centers near Memphis, Tenn., and Southhaven, Miss. Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and other tech giants have spent tens of billions of dollars on their own data center campuses.

The build outs have proved costly. SpaceX said in October that capital expenditures had risen to $19.6 billion during the third quarter, nearly three times its spending from the previous year. Mr. Musk said in October that the company had also closed $40 billion in debt financing to help fund the chips needed for its data centers.

SpaceX’s chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, has said the company will continue to spend heavily on its data center build out. In October, he said the company was likely to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the three months ending in December.

item.title: Microsoft Programs Disrupted by Outage
item.description:
Microsoft reported an outage involving its sprawling set of software tools early Thursday afternoon. The outage has continued for at least three hours, users reported.

Between 12:15 and 1 p.m. Eastern, the outage tracker Downdetector showed that more than 130,000 users were experiencing problems with Microsoft Outlook, which is used for email, calendars and other online tasks. Similar spikes in outages were reported with Microsoft 365, the workplace messaging app Microsoft Teams, the A.I. assistant Microsoft Copilot and the Microsoft Store, Downdetector’s data showed.

By 4 p.m. the number of users reporting issues with Microsoft’s applications had been cut nearly in half.

Microsoft said initially that part of its infrastructure was “experiencing elevated load.”

Later the company said in a social media post that “we determined the elevated load isn’t driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, straining the remaining infrastructure.”

“We’re working to safely return them to service,” Microsoft added in the post.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: Huang and Lutnick Summoned to Testify Before Congress
item.description:
Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee as Mr. Huang’s affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy raises national security concerns.

Senator Tim Scott, Republican of South Carolina, on Thursday evening sent letters to Mr. Huang and Mr. Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee.

“Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology,” Mr. Scott said in a social media post, adding, “The American people deserve answers.”

Congressional leaders of both political parties have said they support efforts to hear from Mr. Huang directly about his entanglement with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. officials concluded had been recruited by China’s main spy agency.

Mr. Scott asked Mr. Huang to appear on Dec. 3 by his own volition but also threatened that the committee could issue a subpoena. House Republicans also said on Thursday they were in discussions with Mr. Huang to testify before other committees. Mr. Huang has hired lawyers who previously represented executives in government investigations, according to people familiar with the matter.

Mr. Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday. But that has not appeared to slow a bipartisan push for more information on whether he had compromised national security.

Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, said in a social media post that Congress must “demand answers” from Mr. Huang. Mr. Schumer also called on the Trump administration to “answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.”

Mr. Lutnick’s department was required to review companies for national security risks before the Trump administration allowed Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China last year. The top Democrats on two congressional committees also wrote to Mr. Lutnick on Thursday, saying they were investigating the matter.

Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the banking committee, said that Mr. Huang’s resignation “does not absolve him, other executives or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws.”

She added in a statement that the company still would “owe Congress answers.” She also demanded that Trump officials “ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China’s military.”

Michael Gold, Ana Swanson and Tony Romm contributed reporting.
